01.note: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, visited the house of Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yosei ben Lakonya. When his hosts offered him a cup of wine, he took it at the first offer and drank it down in one go. They asked whether he did not accept the rule that someone who drinks his cup at one time is a guzzler. He answered that the rule was not said about their small cup, their sweet wine and his wide stomach.
01.why: The Gemara has just told of Rav Huna, son of Rav Natan, who defended each of his manners as a guest, including drinking his cup in two sips because one gulp marks a guzzler; this story shows a guest who drank in one gulp and explained why the rule did not apply to him.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The guest, who drinks his cup of wine in one go.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yosei ben Lakonya
people.about: The host at whose house the visit takes place.

02.note: Ulla, a visitor to Babylonia, came to Pumbedita, and his hosts brought him a basket of dates. He asked how many such baskets a zuz would buy, and they told him three. He exclaimed that a basketful of honey-sweet dates cost a single zuz, and yet the Babylonians did not study Torah more. That night the dates gave him painful indigestion, and he changed his verdict: a basketful of deadly poison sells for a zuz in Babylonia, and still the Babylonians study Torah.
02.why: Ulla has just said that Israel was exiled to Babylonia so they could eat its plentiful dates and so have strength for Torah study; his own experience with those dates is told next.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A visiting Sage who comes to Pumbedita and comments on the Babylonians and their dates.

terms.meaning: A silver coin of the time, used here as a small everyday price.
A town in Babylonia with a center of Torah study.

03.note: A king and queen told their slaves to go and slaughter the Passover offering for them, and the slaves slaughtered two. The slaves asked the king which one to eat; he sent them to the queen, and she sent them to Rabban Gamliel. Rabban Gamliel ruled that a king and queen, who are easy about whatever food is brought to them, should eat from the first one slaughtered. But ordinary people like us, he said, would eat from neither the first nor the second.
03.why: The mishna lets a master who gave no instructions eat from whichever animal his slave slaughtered first, though a baraita says no one may be registered for two Passover offerings at once. The Gemara answers that the mishna means a king and queen, and brings this case as support.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Sage the queen sends the slaves to, who decides which offering the king and queen eat.

people.name: The king
people.about: Sends his slaves to ask the queen.

people.name: The queen
people.about: Sends the slaves on to Rabban Gamliel.

terms.meaning: The lamb or kid slaughtered on the eve of Passover and eaten that night by a group of people who registered for it in advance.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

04.note: Another time, a lizard was found in the royal kitchen, and the staff wanted to declare the whole meal ritually impure. They asked the king, who sent them to the queen, who sent them to Rabban Gamliel. He asked whether the kitchen was hot or cold, and they said hot. He told them to pour a cup of cold liquid on the lizard; they did, it quivered, and Rabban Gamliel declared the entire meal ritually pure.
04.why: This is the second case in a baraita about the same king, queen and Rabban Gamliel, after the one about two Passover offerings. The Gemara's closing remark is that the king depended on the queen, the queen on Rabban Gamliel, and so the whole royal meal depended on him.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who is consulted and declares the meal pure.

people.name: The king
people.about: Sends the question to the queen.

people.name: The queen
people.about: Sends the question on to Rabban Gamliel.

terms.meaning: A religious status, not dirt. The dead body of a creeping creature such as a lizard makes food it touches unfit to eat in a state of purity; a live one does not.

05.note: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, pooled their bread to eat together. By the time Rav Huna ate one piece, Rav Pappa had eaten four. Rav Huna asked to divide the food; Rav Pappa replied that he had accepted the partnership. Rav Huna raised objection after objection, which Rav Pappa answered, until he cited the rule about a shared friendly meal, and Rav Pappa divided the bread with him. Later Rav Huna shared bread with Ravina, who ate eight pieces to his one, and Rav Huna said: better a hundred Pappas than one Ravina.
05.why: The Gemara has concluded that members of a group may not split up for no reason, and that one who eats much more may be told to take his portion and go; this story shows two Sages arguing over exactly that rule at a real meal.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Shares bread with Rav Huna and eats four pieces to his one, then agrees to divide.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Shares bread with Rav Pappa and later with Ravina, and asks each time to divide.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Shares bread with Rav Huna and eats eight pieces to his one.

06.note: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei were reclining at a meal in Akko when Shabbat began. Rabban Shimon asked Rabbi Yosei whether they should stop eating, out of regard for the view of their colleague Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yosei protested that every day Rabban Shimon preferred his rulings over Rabbi Yehuda's, and now he would prefer Rabbi Yehuda's in front of him, quoting a verse from Esther. Rabban Shimon answered that they would not stop, so the students would not see it and fix the law that way for generations. The Sages reported that they did not move from there until they fixed the law as Rabbi Yosei held.
06.why: The Gemara is discussing whether people already eating when Shabbat or a Festival begins must interrupt the meal. A baraita gives the dispute, Rabbi Yehuda says yes and Rabbi Yosei says no, and this story, told in the same baraita, ends with the law fixed like Rabbi Yosei.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: Dines with the two Sages and proposes stopping the meal out of regard for Rabbi Yehuda.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Holds that a meal must be interrupted when Shabbat begins.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Holds that the meal need not be interrupted, and objects to giving way to Rabbi Yehuda.

terms.meaning: A title of honor for a distinguished man, used by Rabban Shimon in addressing Rabbi Yosei.
A town on the coast of the Land of Israel, where the meal took place.

07.note: Rav Huna once recited kiddush, and then his lamp went out. Since eating in the dark was hard, he moved his belongings to the wedding house of his son Rabba, where there was a lamp. There he recited kiddush again and ate something.
07.why: Shmuel holds that kiddush counts only where one eats the Shabbat meal. The Gemara argues that Rav Huna held the same, since he said kiddush again when he moved to another house to eat.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Recites kiddush, loses his light, and recites it again where he eats.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Rav Huna's son, at whose wedding house there was a lamp.

terms.meaning: The blessing that marks the start of Shabbat, usually said over a cup of wine before the evening meal.

08.note: Rav Beruna and Rav Hananel, students of Rav, were eating together while Rav Yeiva the Elder served them. They asked him for a cup so they could recite Grace after Meals, then changed their minds and asked for a cup to drink. He told them that Rav had said that once they asked for the cup for Grace, they were forbidden to drink, because they had turned their minds away from drinking.
08.why: Rava told this story to explain to his guest Rav Ya'akov bar Abba why he said the wine blessing again over the cup of Grace after Meals: like Rav's students, he held that getting ready for Grace ends the earlier blessing on wine.

people.name: Rav Beruna
people.about: One of Rav's students at the meal.

people.name: Rav Hananel
people.about: One of Rav's students at the meal.

people.name: Rav Yeiva the Elder
people.about: Serves the students and tells them what Rav said.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The teacher whose ruling Rav Yeiva the Elder reports.

terms.meaning: The blessings said after eating a meal with bread, sometimes over a cup of wine.

09.note: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi were eating together while Rav Aha, son of Rava, served them. Ameimar said the wine blessing over every cup, Mar Zutra over the first cup and the last, and Rav Ashi over the first cup only. Rav Aha asked them whose practice he should follow. Ameimar said he kept changing his mind, meaning each cup was meant to be his last, and Mar Zutra said he followed the students of Rav. Rav Ashi's reply comes in the discussion that follows.
09.why: Just before this, Rava used a ruling from Rav's students to explain why he blessed the wine again after Grace after Meals. Here three later Sages each do it differently, and Mar Zutra names Rav's students as his source.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: Blesses every cup, because each time he meant it to be his last.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: Blesses the first and last cups, following the students of Rav.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Blesses only the first cup.

people.name: Rav Aha, son of Rava
people.about: Serves the three Sages and asks whose practice to follow.

terms.meaning: Rav's disciples, who held that once you prepare for Grace after Meals, you must bless any further wine again.

10.note: Rav Ya'akov bar Abba was a guest at Rava's house. When it was time for havdala, Rava's attendant lit a torch from a candle. The guest asked why, when a candle was already there; Rava said the attendant did it on his own; the guest replied that he would not have done it without hearing it from Rava, and Rava asked whether he did not agree that a torch is the best way to do it. Rava then said havdala, listing four distinctions, and his guest asked why so many, since Rav had called the single phrase between sacred and profane Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's havdala. Rava answered with a rule of at least three and at most seven distinctions, and explained that the fourth was not a separate one but a phrase echoing the blessing's ending.
10.why: The Gemara stopped to discuss the ruling of Rav's students that Rava had cited earlier in this same visit; now it goes back to the visit and carries on with Rava's havdala.

people.name: Rav Ya'akov bar Abba
people.about: A guest at Rava's house who questions each step of his havdala.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The host, who defends how he recites havdala.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Named by Rav as having said only the single distinction between sacred and profane.

terms.meaning: The blessing that marks the end of Shabbat, said over a cup of wine, with a blessing over fire and listing the 'distinctions' God made, such as between sacred and profane.

terms.term: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said
terms.meaning: The usual Talmudic way of passing on a teaching: one Sage repeats in the name of his teacher what that teacher said.

11.note: When Ulla visited Pumbedita, Rav Yehuda told his son Rav Yitzhak to bring Ulla a basket of fruit and see how he recited havdala. Rav Yitzhak did not go himself but sent Abaye, who reported that Ulla said only, Blessed is He Who distinguishes between sacred and profane. When Rav Yitzhak told his father that he had sent Abaye instead, Rav Yehuda told him that his haughtiness and pride had made sure the teaching would not be passed on in his name.
11.why: The Gemara is asking how havdala should end and has ruled like Shmuel, who ends it with the words who distinguishes between sacred and profane; this story shows Ulla using that phrase, and the next objection in the discussion is to his practice.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A visiting Sage whose havdala Rav Yehuda wants observed.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Rav Yitzhak's father, who sends him to watch Ulla and rebukes him for not going.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak
people.about: Rav Yehuda's son, who sends Abaye in his place.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Goes in Rav Yitzhak's place and reports how Ulla recited havdala.

terms.meaning: The blessing that marks the end of Shabbat, separating the holy day from the ordinary week.
A town in Babylonia with a center of Torah study.

12.note: Rav Hananya bar Shelemya and other students of Rav were eating a meal on Shabbat eve while Rav Hamnuna the Elder served them. They asked him to go and see whether Shabbat had begun, so they could stop and start the meal again as a Shabbat meal. He told them there was no need, because Shabbat sets the meal by itself, citing Rav. They concluded that the end of Shabbat likewise requires havdala in the middle of a meal, but Rav Amram told them Rav had said Shabbat sets the duty of kiddush, not of havdala.
12.why: The Gemara is discussing havdala and the meals around Shabbat; right after this story it adds that one need not stop an ongoing meal for havdala, but may not begin a new one before it.

people.name: Rav Hananya bar Shelemya
people.about: One of Rav's students eating the meal.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna the Elder
people.about: Serves the students and tells them Shabbat sets the meal by itself.

people.name: Rav Amram
people.about: Corrects the students' conclusion about havdala, citing Rav.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The teacher whose rulings are quoted.

terms.meaning: The blessing that marks the start of Shabbat, said over a cup of wine before eating.
The blessing that marks the end of Shabbat.
Portions of produce that must be set aside for priests, Levites and the poor before the food may be eaten as a regular meal.

13.note: Rav Ashi came to the city of Mehoza, and on Shabbat day the locals asked him to recite the great kiddush for them and handed him a cup of wine. Not sure what they meant, he reasoned that every blessing over a cup begins with Who creates the fruit of the vine, so he said that and drew it out. When he saw an old man bend over and drink, he understood that this was the whole of it, and applied to himself the verse, The wise man, his eyes are in his head.
13.why: Rav Yehuda has just ruled that the daytime kiddush on Shabbat is only the usual blessing over wine; the story shows the people of Mehoza calling that plain blessing the great kiddush.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A visiting Sage asked to recite the great kiddush, who works out what is expected of him.

people.name: The elder
people.about: An old man whose drinking shows Rav Ashi that the blessing is complete.

terms.meaning: A blessing over wine that marks the holiness of Shabbat; the daytime one is shorter than the one said on Friday night.
A town in Babylonia.

14.note: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba was a guest at Rav Asi's house. After Shabbat he forgot and tasted some food before havdala; he was given a cup and recited havdala anyway. Rav Asi's wife said to her husband that he did not do it that way. Rav Asi told her to leave him alone, since he followed the view of his own teacher.
14.why: The Gemara has just reported a dispute: Rav Huna said one who has eaten may still recite havdala, and Rav Asi said one may not. The story shows Rav Asi tolerating a guest who followed the other view.

people.name: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba
people.about: A guest who eats before havdala and then recites it.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: The host, who holds that one who has eaten may not recite havdala.

people.name: Rav Asi's wife
people.about: Points out that her husband does not act this way.

terms.meaning: The blessing that marks the end of Shabbat; one is not supposed to eat before saying it.

15.note: Mar Yanuka and Mar Kashisha, sons of Rav Hisda, told Rav Ashi that Ameimar once visited them when they had no wine. They brought him beer; he would not recite havdala over it and went to sleep fasting. The next day they went to the trouble of bringing wine, and he recited havdala and ate. The following year he came again, they again had only beer, and he said that if so, beer is the wine of the province, recited havdala over it and ate.
15.why: Rava has just ruled that one who missed havdala on Saturday night may say it later; the Gemara then draws three rulings from Ameimar's behavior and goes on to ask whether beer may be used for kiddush or havdala.

people.name: Mar Yanuka
people.about: A son of Rav Hisda who tells the story to Rav Ashi.

people.name: Mar Kashisha
people.about: A son of Rav Hisda who tells the story to Rav Ashi.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage the brothers tell the story to.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: A Sage who visits the brothers twice and must decide whether to recite havdala over beer.

terms.meaning: The blessing that marks the end of Shabbat, normally said over wine; one may not eat until it is said.
A drink that serves as the local wine where real wine is hard to get, and so may stand in for it in a blessing.

16.note: Levi sent Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi a beer of thirteen soakings, a strong, high-quality brew. He tasted it and found it very pleasant, saying that such a drink was fit to recite kiddush over and to say over it all the songs and praises in the world. That night it caused him pain, and he said: it pains and then it soothes.
16.why: The Gemara has just reported that kiddush and havdala may not be said over date beer; this story about a fine beer leads into a series of Sages' remarks on the harm beer causes and whether it may be used for kiddush.

people.name: Levi
people.about: Sends the beer to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi in the text; tastes and praises the beer, then suffers from it.

terms.meaning: The blessing that marks the holiness of Shabbat, normally said over wine.
A beer made by soaking thirteen batches of dates in the same water, so that it took on a strong flavor.

17.note: A man divorced his wife, and she married a shopkeeper who sold wine. Every day the first husband came to the shop to drink, and she worked witchcraft against him, but it had no effect because he was careful never to drink an even number of cups. One day he drank a great deal: up to sixteen cups he kept count, but after that he lost track, and she sent him off after an even number. On the road an Arab saw him and said: a dead man is walking here. He went and hugged a palm tree; the palm tree dried out, and he burst.
17.why: The Gemara has said that against harmful spirits only certain numbers of things in pairs are dangerous, but against witchcraft one must worry even about larger even numbers. This story shows that: the witchcraft worked once the man drank an even number of cups beyond sixteen.

people.name: The man
people.about: A divorced husband who drinks daily in his ex-wife's new husband's shop.

people.name: His ex-wife
people.about: Now married to a wine-seller; works witchcraft against her former husband.

people.name: The Arab
people.about: A passerby who sees he is bewitched and calls him a dead man.

terms.meaning: The belief, discussed here, that doing things in even numbers, such as drinking an even number of cups, exposes a person to demons and witchcraft.

18.note: A Torah scholar once went to relieve himself near a caper bush, where a demon lives. He heard the demon coming at him and fled. As the demon went, it grabbed hold of a palm tree; the palm tree dried out, and the demon burst.
18.why: The Gemara is listing the demons that live near certain plants and why it matters; it says the caper-bush demon has no eyes, which matters for fleeing from it, and this story shows a scholar escaping it that way.

people.name: The Torah scholar
people.about: Flees the demon near the caper bush.

terms.meaning: A thorny shrub. The Gemara says a demon with no eyes lives near it.

19.note: A city official went and stood near a sorb tree close to the city, and sixty demons came upon him, putting his life in danger. One of the Sages, who did not know the tree held sixty demons, wrote him an amulet against a single demon. The man then heard the demons celebrating inside the tree and singing that the master wears a scholar's scarf but does not know how to say the blessing. Another Sage, who knew it was a tree of sixty demons, wrote an amulet against sixty, and the man heard them saying: clear your things out of here.
19.why: The Gemara has said that the sorb tree near a city holds no fewer than sixty demons, which matters when writing an amulet; this story shows an amulet failing for want of that knowledge and working with it.

people.name: The city official
people.about: Stands by the sorb tree and is put in danger by sixty demons.

people.name: The first Sage
people.about: Writes an amulet against one demon, not knowing there are sixty.

people.name: The second Sage
people.about: Knows the tree holds sixty demons and writes an amulet against all of them.

terms.meaning: A written charm worn for protection against demons or illness.
A kind of tree that the Gemara says demons live near.

20.note: Abaye was walking along with Rav Pappa on his right and Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, on his left. He saw a demon called ketev meriri approaching on his left, so he switched them, moving Rav Pappa to his left and Rav Huna to his right. Rav Pappa asked why Abaye was not worried about him. Abaye answered: the time is in your favor.
20.why: The Gemara has just described the ketev meriri, a demon that comes before noon; this story shows a Sage seeing one and protecting a companion from it.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sees the demon and moves his companions around.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Walks beside Abaye and is moved to the side where the demon is coming.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Walks beside Abaye and is moved away from the demon.

terms.meaning: A demon named in the Torah; the Gemara says it comes before noon.
